utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start the main business of the day, there's a matter that I have to raise that would be of concern to the Trial Chamber as much as it is to assigned counsel. We're all aware of the recent litigation there has been over the appointment of assigned counsel, and decisions have been made at various stages of the process consistent with examining that position. I have to tell the Trial Chamber that specific terms and conditions were agreed with the Registry for our engagement as assigned counsel, and it was on those terms that we undertook the assignment. On the 3rd of December, the Registry issued a letter to us revoking what had previously been agreed and imposing completely new terms and conditions unilaterally upon us in the absence of any consultation or agreement. This is a matter of great concern, because it completely repudiates what had been arranged with assigned counsel and puts us in a very difficult personal position. In effect, it totally undermines the order of this Court appointing us as assigned counsel, and it's probably an attack on the position that the Trial Chamber would have least expected and least welcomed. We are very concerned. I responded on the 6th of December, asking -- or refusing to accept those changes in our conditions, and there were meetings last week, but I was told that those conditions applied anyway. We are greatly concerned, and I have told them that they have by Friday to reimpose the conditions or, by agreement, vary conditions, because that description I gave to the Trial Chamber of the Registrar being hauled up to explain himself is capable of actually occurring. I've told them that if they are going to do that, I have no option but to seek work elsewhere from January of 2005, because it completely undermines the position of assigned Defence counsel in this case, and I would have thought was an attack on the position that the Trial Chamber would least welcome. I have to raise this matter because this is of great importance. It concerns our personal commitment to the case, and we have not accepted any variation in terms. We would do or may do if they were appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, isn't this a matter that, if you wish us to consider, you should be filing a motion? I don't know that the Chamber is in a position to do anything unless there is a motion filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've raised it orally. I have considered that, whether I do -- I did that and whether I produce correspondence to you, as I didn't know whether the Court wanted to get into the detail of it, because traditionally this has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we had a motion, we could look at it and then I think we'd have to consider to what extent we are competent to deal with the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the moment it's contractual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we can deal with it orally. I wouldn't like to attempt to deal with it orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a contractual matter at the moment, and for that reason I am very concerned about the unilateral overturning of agreements without consultation, which are guaranteed to put me in conflict with this Registry and this Court. They know that. We are absolutely furious about this matter, because it -- there's a lot of personal commitment riding on our involvement, and the one thing that's guaranteed to destroy our position and make me make a personal decision, which it seems to be unnecessary on that basis, would be that, and they know that, and we are astonished about what has gone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, as I indicated, the Chamber is of the view that, if you wish, this is a matter in respect of which you should consider filing a motion for us to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But we don't think it proper to debate the matter in Court in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand that. I have to raise things in the issue of transparency, otherwise the Court will think that I have done something completely without any motivation, which is simply not the case. And I felt so strongly about it that it should be raised so that you knew of it today. The end of the legal term is Friday, and January 2005 is arriving, and people should not be treated in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing it to our attention, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness Professor Popov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Popov, you are still subject to the declaration that you made. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, would you take a look at your report, please, page 37. And in the English it is page 34 going over to page 35. But for you in the Serbian language, it is page 37.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The third paragraph begins as follows: "The crushing of the Greater Serbia policy during World War I was brought to the level of widespread war crimes, persecution and even threats of extinction of the Serbian people." Now, what can you tell us about that? What do historical facts say about that? How do they stand?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can quote a few examples. The first genocidal, if I can put it that way, action was carried out in Bosnia in August 1914 at a place called Celebici where 84 Serb civilians were shot. After that, there were mass arrests of the Serb population, and especially in Bosnia. We see prominent intellectuals, businessmen, tradesmen arrested. And two trials were organised in Banja Luka in 1915 in which heavy sentences were meted out for many years imprisonment, for the simple fact that the people arrested and accused were prominent public figures, politicians in Bosnia itself. And at the same time - may I just be allowed to finish? - in Vojvodina there were also mass arrests were people were taken to concentration camps, and among others we saw very prominent individuals like the leader of the Radical Party, Jasa Tomic, and a prominent scientist, Vasa Stajic, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the following page, which is in your text page 38 and carries on in the English on page 35, you mentioned what happened on the territory of the then-Austria-Hungary.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you end this paragraph by saying: "The most hideous war crimes against the civilian population were committed in the occupied parts of Serbia in 1914 and were repeated in the second phase of the occupation between 1915 to 1918."

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In the occupied parts of Serbia in 1914, in the autumn, that is to say after the first battle of Cer when the Austrian army was expelled from Serbia and when the second offensive began at the time of the so-called battle of Kolubara, there were large-scale Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond crimes committed against the civilian population, and very often the victims were women. And there is extensive written matter and photographs about that. Several villages were destroyed. Among other things, the town of Sabac was seriously destroyed, and we have much testimony about that from the prominent Swiss legal man Wilhelm Reiss [phoen], and for that he was given great recognition in Serbia. So that Austrian occupation, the first occupation, which lasted until December 1914 was remembered by the most terrible crimes in which several thousand people were killed. However, later on, after the second occupation, when the Germans beat the Serbian army in 1915, the autumn of that year, then there was permanent terror over the whole of the occupied territories, especially in Toplica in 1917 after an uprising against the Bulgarian authorities when the Austrians came as reinforcements and when the people of Kursumlija, Prokuplje and other areas and villages suffered enormous losses. All in all, the losses numbered there thousands. We don't have exact records of them and figures of them, and men of science have not counted all the victims yet, and I don't think they'll ever manage to do so to the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you've now quoted examples from Bosnia, from Serbia, from the first occupation and from the second occupation, and in the following paragraph of your report, you say: "All this, from the Austro-Hungarian annexation policy through German offensive plans to war crimes, was obscured by the (war cries) against the Greater Serbia policy with its alleged 'conspiracy' and 'criminal plans.' One must not forget that at the same time, the scenario of castigating 'Greater Serbian nationalism' was continued after World War I by those who lost the war and the revisionist countries of the defeated camp." Therefore, everything was justified, as you yourself say here, by the outcries against Greater Serbian nationalism, plots, conspiracies, and so on. Now, as an historian, can you draw a parallel between what was done then and what is being done today, to the present day, because here in this courtroom, in this room we're once again hearing the term "Greater Serbian nationalism" being bandied about and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... invitation to the witness to comment on what's happening in Court. By all means the witness may conceivably, I suppose, answer some questions about evidence, but it looks to me as though this question was actually focusing on the Court itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I think it's focusing on the evidence that has been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just reformulate your question to make it clearer that what you're asking the witness to do is to comment on the evidence that has been given in Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had just asked Professor Popov to comment on what he says in his report, the statement he made. And if we were to simplify it, then in what I've just quoted, this would indicate that the mass crimes and genocide perpetrated against the Serbs were justified throughout by some sort of Greater Serbian nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not to make statements like that when you're asking a question. Just reformulate the question. Professor Popov, I think the question that is being asked is whether the evidence that has been given in Court about the concept of a Greater Serbia bears any parallel with what happened in the -- is it the 1914, 1915, Mr. Milosevic? In the First World War. Do you see any parallel? I'm interested in the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be difficult for me to say that there were none, that you cannot draw any parallels, especially in rhetorics; and secondly, in the methods of explaining Serbian history, that is to say, looking at it in the past, 100 years ago, 90 years ago during World War I, and in the last decades of the 20th century. The explanation given was always that Serbia had aggressive plans towards its neighbours, for instance, that it wished to appropriate other people's territory, and that the goal was to create a Greater Serbian state in which it would include other -- the members of other ethnic groups and nations. So the parallel there is quite obvious and evident. Of course I cannot comment about things that went on here in the courtroom because I wasn't here to follow the proceedings, the whole trial. However, in public, the general public opinion is that in the moves made by the great powers towards Serbia, the parallels drawn there are more than evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When you go on to speak about, in your report -- actually, you say: "German and Central-European clerical accusations against the 'Greater Serbia threat' found their most devoted followers and clique in Croatian chauvinists of all hues in Croatia. And the Greater Croatia aspirations allegedly from a threat of Greater Serbian was a formidable screen, a means of camouflage." Now, why do you speak of a screen and camouflage? Why do you use those terms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you started out well in terms of adhering to the practice of alerting the Chamber to the page in the report that you are citing. What is the page and where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, 34, 35. This is paragraph at the beginning of page 35, "German and Central European clerical accusations," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] German Imperialism, which was being created and was being geared towards East-central Europe and Eastern Europe, gained expression particularly at the end of the 19th century, the last decades of the 19th century, in fact, and at the beginning of the 20th century, before the First World War. This German Imperialistic breakthrough "Drang nach Osten," to the east was pushed by Austria, which had a twofold motivation for this, for breaking through to the Balkans and for attacking Serbia, and it was this: The burgeoning of the liberation tendencies of the South Slav peoples within their borders, which looked to a free Serbia; and secondly, the strategic position of Serbia through which you had to pass and surmount if you wanted to move further to the east and open the road to Celonica [phoen] and Constantinople and the other. Now, with this Austrian breakthrough we saw the Croatian efforts and aspirations latch onto it. Not, of course, all the Croatian people, but a significant portion of the political leadership or the political public opinion which was very loud, represented by clerical Catholic circles and the so-called Party of Rights, first and foremost, and then the genuine Party of Rights, Stranka Prava. That is to say the clerical Ivan Frank followers, because Ivan Frank and Josip Frank led the party, and they were preparing a large march on Serbia on the one hand, and on the other hand they were preparing to destroy the Serb population in Croatia proper. And they even went so far as to organise some volunteer detachments which would have as their task a settling of accounts with Serbs in Croatia because they were afraid of their operations and action in the rear. With a Prince Cuvaj, who was not favourably disposed to the Serbs, I think that in 1910 we had a deputy from the Franko Fatima's party, so Krsnjavi, he went as a representative and deputy and proposed that the Serbian question in Croatia be dealt with first of all and resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because I don't think we need all of that detail. We just need an outline of the main historical points of interest. I don't think we need all of that detail. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mr. Milosevic, let's concentrate on the important points in this history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, sorry. There was no translation of your question, Mr. Milosevic, so please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you hear the English channel now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you described Frank's supporters as clerical fascists. That's the definition you use in your text. Why?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were opposed to parliamentary democracy and they were advocating a Greater Croatian policy on ethnic grounds, saying that the Croatian nation was the only decisive factor in Croatian politics. They asked for the extermination of Serbs, that they should be killed by axes in the head. That was the terminology they used. The Catholic church always supported them and in a way gave them ideological and religious support. To this kind of policy, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's get things clear here. In your paper, you do not talk about the Croatian people. On the contrary, you talk about Croatian chauvinists only.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's be clear on that. Who was Ivo Pilar?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Pilar was a writer, a member or at least a supporter of Frank's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now, what do you know about his theory of the indispensability of eradicating Greater Serbdom? You referred to it on the same page. "The eradication of Greater Serbdom as the bearer of an inferior Eastern Byzantine civilisation." I'm quoting you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sudland was the pseudonym he used when, in 1915, he published a book in which he proved that -- or set out to prove that a Greater Serbian policy was actually infringing upon harmonious relations in the Balkans and preventing the penetration of the Western civilisation because they were traditionally linked to the Eastern church and the Byzantine historical heritage. This was a major obstacle to the spread of Roman Catholicism on the one hand and the Western civilisation in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we now are hearing of a Greater Croatian policy. We have heard of a Greater Albanian policy, and of course a Greater Serbian policy. The only thing missing now is a Greater Bosnian policy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you'll have to ask the professor to explain that for you if that's the only thing you still have missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It appears that all the states in the region had expansionist visions at one time or another.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You've put this very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbia have expansionist aspirations, or what was the word that Mr. Robinson used?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia did not. Serbia had its national programme which envisaged the creation of a national state. That was an aspiration that meant keeping abreast of the times. That is what all nations wanted at the time, to keep abreast of the times. This was the process of modernisation in Europe at the end of the 19th and the beginning of the 20th century. There could not have been a Greater Bosnian programme because a Bosnian nation did not exist. I can just give you one piece of information: The Bosnian Muslims, from 1860 until 1980, changed their ethnic affiliation nine times -- ten times, from Turkish to Muslim. So there could not have been a Greater Bosnian programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't dwell too much on it. It was a lighthearted comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, in order to make things clear, could you please put on the overhead projector, that is in tab 5, actually. This is a collection of documents. As soon as you open page 1, you have a letter of Frano Supilo.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sent to Sir Edward Grey.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: London, 30th of September, 1915. So could you please put this on the ELMO. We're not going to go through the entire letter, just a few sentences so that they can be interpreted. So point 1, Supilo says: "Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes are genetically one nation with three names of different historical, legal, state traditions but of one language and belonging to one race." So he is talking about one nation, one people with three names. Vuk Karadzic, considerably before, that speaks of one people and three laws; Greek law, Roman law, and Turkish law. Speaking of people belonging to three laws, he actually refers to the three faiths, the three religions. Tell me now, this approach of a single people, to what extent did it come to the fore during these years of crisis at the end of the 19th century, beginning of the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea of the unity of the Southern Slav peoples is not a Serb idea. It is an idea of a still undifferentiated and still nationally undefined people of Croatia, the Croatian people. It is called the Illyrian Movement. After that, the idea of the unity of the three people in one, Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, was a very widespread one in the political and intellectual public. And at first, it had a rather cool reception in the Serbian public. The Serbs espoused this idea only towards the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th century. Supilo, as you can see, was a supporter of this idea and theory himself, that is to say, of the national unity of the Southern Slavs, at least the ethnic unity of the Southern Slavs, except that they were divided by religion and history. Vuk Karadzic, while accepting the Illyrian idea, believed that this unity was based on linguistic unity, which in Central Europe was present in Central Europe, and even now linguistic theory believes that language is the most prominent feature of a people, a nation. So it was at least in the philological and cultural circles that the Serbs did espouse this theory. It was the end of the 19th century, the beginning of the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would like to hear from the professor the meaning of Serbislav people. Could you elaborate on the meaning. I think he mentioned Serbislav people, which I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Serb Slav language, which is Slavonic, Slavonic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation doesn't read right. Slavono-Serb. This is Slavonic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Slavonic language was the literary language of the Serbs before Vuk Karadzic's reform in the mid-19th century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is now clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, Supilo says: "The idea of national unity of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes from a political point of view brings a logical consequence; the aspiration to unite into a single free state in which each tribe would -- with its own name and its own traditions will bring its best abilities and powers into this new state." Not to waste time, in number 6, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my mistake, I'm sure, but I can't immediately find the paragraph 4 to which the accused is referring. And Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond if it is -- if it is Roman IV on the right-hand side of the letter of Edward Grey, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, redirect us to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roman numeral IV. Yes, Roman numeral IV, the letter of Frano Supilo to Sir Edward Grey, 30th of September, 1915. So the first quotation was Roman numeral I, and then there is a footnote, and then on the right-hand side numerals II through V are printed. So I've already quoted them, the idea of the national unity of Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in number VI, it says on the same page: "If forces stronger than fairness want to stop the implementation of this fair idea, that is to say, for example, that they wish to exclude Croatia from this framework of Yugoslav countries with Serbia, then -- and to create a separate State of Croatia, then it is necessary that Serbia at first carry out the necessary reforms, national, political, constitutional, cultural, which would make it impossible to develop another competitive Yugoslav state as well as every national work-force. In other words, it is necessary to have Serbia reformed internally in such a way that it should be the only proponent of the unity of Yugoslavs." What can we see on the basis of this, Professor?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that Frano Supilo, belonging to the Croatian-Serbian coalition said that it was necessary to have this kind of unity and to link up the Serbs and Croats so that the Croats would not be separated from the other Southern Slavs, notably the Serbs, because in that case, there would be antagonism between them, a competitive struggle which would work to the detriment of both peoples. That is why he asked for the support of the great powers, notably Great Britain, believing that that is the only fair solution, to use his words, and that the great powers will not turn a deaf ear to this historical justice of bringing the two peoples together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please take tab 3 now. This is one of the few exhibits that have been translated. The Nis declaration. Unfortunately, the Corfu declaration has not been translated, I think. It's within the same documents that we quoted a few minutes ago. But in the Nis declaration, on the 24th of November, it's a single page.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 7th of December, according to the new calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the 7th of December, 24th of November. In paragraph 4 -- the first paragraph is only one line -- it says: "In these decisive moments, the only task to --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the speaker to please slow down because they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to speak more slowly. Why don't they have the text? Because we have it here --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it, and I assume that they have it, because they should have this same set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do the interpreters have this? I'm asking the Deputy Registrar. We're just checking to ensure that they have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that I can proceed. You have the text in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we also want the interpreters to have it. Do the interpreters now have the text?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in paragraph IV, I'm quoting paragraph IV of the Nis declaration, where it says: "The government of the kingdom considers as its most important and only task in these crucial moments to ensure the successful outcome of this great struggle which, at the moment when it started, became the struggle for the liberation and unification of all our unfree brothers; Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes." So this is the very beginning of the war, 1914. What is the approach of Serbia's policy at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of this declaration, a very solemn declaration adopted by the national Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbia is that the Kingdom of Serbia is waging a war for two primary objectives: For the defence of the homeland, that is to say, their own fatherland, the Kingdom of Serbia, but it is not waging it for the creation of a Greater Serbia or taking territories that were populated mostly by Serbs. On the contrary, they are waging a struggle coinciding with the wishes of the other Southern Slavic peoples, notably the Croats and Slovenes. Serbia is waging a struggle for their emancipation from Austro-Hungarian rule and for the creation of a joint state of three equal peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, now please go back to tab 5. After the documents that I quoted already, there is the Corfu declaration adopted in July 1917.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is rather long. And this is where elements are given of the future state establishment, but what is the historical importance of the Corfu declaration? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows that the idea of creating a joint state had spread to large numbers of Serbian, Croatian, and Slovenian members of the public and that they were willing to enter into a joint state with Serbia, even sacrificing some of their own ideas. The Yugoslav council was an organisation of Croatian, Serb, and Slovenian emigres from Austria, and its principles were to create a so-called dual federation. Serbia did not wish to agree to this but asked that a unified state be created where all religious, national, and other rights of all three peoples would be respected. The Croatian and Slovenian politicians accepted this gladly, because they knew that if they did not enter into Yugoslavia together with Serbia, they would experience the tragic fate of defeated nations, because they had been part of Austria-Hungary on the one hand and on the other hand they would have large territorial losses to Italy and Austria, who were defending their territories in the war and who wanted -- so together with Serbia, they wanted to avoid the fate of conquered peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please turn to the next page where you have the statement of Nikola Pasic, the Prime Minister, to The Morning Post. This was not only an interview, it was a public statement, not merely an interview. I cannot quote extensively because it has not been translated. It has been provided only in Serbian in this book of documents, so I wish to draw your attention to the first paragraph, where Pasic first says that the Serbian government will decisively adhere to the Corfu declaration. At the end of the passage he says the following: "The Serbian people cannot not wish to take up a dominant position in the future kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes."

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pasic sincerely thought this. Most Serbian politicians were more than willing to make a number of sacrifices in addition to those they had suffered during the war, and those were enormous for the small state of Serbia. They were willing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, now that you're speaking of this, what were the sacrifices for Serbia in that war?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia lost between a 1.2 million and 1.3 million inhabitants, among them between 350 and 400.000 were soldiers, and the rest were civilians. They severed terror and epidemics, so that the population was reduced by about 30 per cent. The population of Serbia itself, that is, Serbia proper. However, do you wish me to complete my response to the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I just made a small digression in order to show clearly how enormous had been the sacrifices of Serbia, which lost a third of its population in World War I.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The biggest sacrifice that Serbia was willing to make was to renounce its sovereign kingdom of Serbia, which was internationally recognised, and to sink its statehood into the general, more extensive Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond state. They had capital which they were willing to exchange for a loan, an insecure loan. Serbia could have enjoyed great prestige after World War I. In the new state, it risked losing the prestige it had won in World War I, and unfortunately this was to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Pasic goes on to say, in the third passage: "I hereby solemnly declare that Serbia feels it --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is tab number 5.7. You have to indicate the tab number if you'd like the documents to be properly translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, what you have just said is correct. Tab 5.7, the statement of Nikola Pasic in The Morning Post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Serbia feels it its national duty to liberate Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. When they are free, their right to self-determination will be recognised, that is, the right to state freely whether they wish to join Serbia on the basis of the Corfu declaration or whether they wish to create small states as they had done in the distant past. In accordance to what came previously, we not only do not wish to wage an Imperialist policy, we even do not wish to limit the rights of the Serbs, Slovenes, and Croats in any way or even to adhere to the Corfu declaration should it go against their wishes." So he's bringing into question even the Corfu declaration, putting in the first place the wish of these people, once they have been liberated, to make their own choice freely. And the statement of the Yugoslav parliamentary club testifies to the fact that we all agree in our aspirations, as far as our national future goes, and this will be confirmed in an even more solemn manner, and so on and so forth. Can we speak at all of Greater Serbia pretensions, domination, or anything that might in any way cast doubt on the actions and the policy that was implemented?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a scholar, I'm deeply convinced that this was not the case, and that is why I said so in the text that I forwarded to the Court. During World War I, the Serbian government waged an action of liberation, leaving the decision as to whether they would unite with Serbia or not to the authorised representatives of the Croatian and Slovenian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popov, thank you. Tell me now, please, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the professor a question. Professor, then your evidence is that at no time was there ever a Greater Serbian policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, during my first exposition here, I said that there had been such ideas but that they always belonged to peripheral and marginal political forces with one exception, when an organisation of officers demanded a Greater Serbia. There is something that would require a more extensive explanation, three minutes by your leave, when Serbia expressed a certain measure of expansionism viewed from today's point of view. In 1912, Serbian waged the first Balkan war, together with Greece, Montenegro, and Bulgaria in order to expel the Turks from the Southern Slav territories in the Balkans where they had still remained after 1878. One of the most important goals of Serbia in that war was to break through to the Adriatic Sea, because over 80 per cent of its exports were passing through Austria-Hungary, as were its imports. And whenever Austria wanted to exert pressure on Serbia, it would close off the border. For this reason, an Adriatic port was a crucial issue for Serbia. That's why the Serbs wanted to take not only liberated Kosovo but also a port in Northern Albania. As the great powers did not allow this, it took a part of Macedonia, which, seen from today's vantage point, is not Serbian. However, in the early 20th century, the Macedonian nation had not yet constituted itself, and they opted to be either Bulgarian or Serbian at various points or nationally not affiliated. So that the Bulgarians and the Serbs divided up Macedonia and Greece, and they took various parts of Macedonia. This was the only expansionist move by Serbia as far as I know, but I will conclude now by saying, by your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area in the Vardar valley of Macedonia, which had been taken by Serbia, speaking only of the territory where the Serbian army had come, that's where the Macedonian nation and the Macedonian state were established in about 20 years. However, Macedonians are not recognised even as minorities either in Bulgaria or in Greece. In Serbia, they were able to attain affirmation as a nation, to assert themselves, and in this way, the Serbs atoned for the fact that they had not realised on time that these were a separate nation. Had they not done this, Macedonia would not exist today. It would still be divided among Greece, Bulgaria, and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let's clarify just one fact. Today's Republic of Macedonia exists exclusively on the territory liberated from the Turks by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It does not exist outside that territory?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only does Macedonia not exist on those territories, but Macedonians don't exist either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, Macedonia decided to be independent, and without any conflicts nobody tried to prevent this, just as they would not have prevented others had they wished to do so without a conflict.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, to clarify, would you explain: At the end of World War I, did Serbia have an opportunity, although we have seen that it didn't do this, but did it have an opportunity to create a state that might be called Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did have an opportunity to establish a Serbia far larger than Serbia actually was at the time, that is, within borders which would practically double its territory. And the Serbs would still have between 60 and 70 per cent of the population on that territory. These were the borders which the great powers in 1915 offered Serbia for two reasons. In August 1915, pressure was exerted on Serbia by Great Britain and France and Russia to cede to the Bulgarians parts of Eastern Macedonia so that they would be prevented from joining Germany and Austro-Hungary. On the other hand, the London agreement saw the light of day by which the powers of the entente attracted Italy to join them, and this caused protests among the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. As compensation, Serbia was offered the opportunity of creating a state on the territory of Bosnia, parts of Vojvodina without Banat, and Eastern Slavonia. There is even a map which I have to say I believe is a combination of the various offers made by Great Britain and France. Edward Grey and Georges Clemenceau are mentioned by name. Therefore, the first offer to create a Greater Serbia was made to Serbia by the allied powers in World War I. This was the real idea of a Greater Serbia, and I might say the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just make a small digression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we go on, I'm aware, of course, that we challenged aspects of this witness's evidence and the Chamber ruled against us, and of course there has been reference by witnesses called by the Prosecution to Greater Serbia, thus the topic of Greater Serbia generally, but I must invite the Chamber to consider whether we are now going into historical matters in far more detail than can be of any ultimate value to the Chamber. I'm hesitant about interrupting and trying to stop the evidence, because it obviously does no damage to the Prosecution case, but there is the question of the use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is something that the Chamber has in mind. Mr. Milosevic, I think I have said before that we are not in academia. It is proper for you to bring evidence on this question because Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Prosecution made it an important part of their case, and to that extent it is proper for you to bring evidence, but I think we are reaching a stage where we might become drowned in history. You must move us forward to modern times. Fast forward to modern times. I think we have heard enough about the history of this concept, and I don't think the Chamber is going to benefit from more evidence on the 1914-1915 era. So fast forward to the modern era.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will take your suggestion. Of course it is a very rational one, but please bear in mind that one of the main arguments of this false indictment is a criminal enterprise to create a Greater Serbia. This absurdity has to be clarified and debunked. It doesn't deserve anything else. So you will not be harmed by broader and more extensive knowledge of the issues on which this false indictment is based. These historical facts are indisputable. I just wanted to make a digression. You might call this a detail, but Mr. Nice, for example, put forward this detail in a certain telephone conversation, allegedly between Karadzic and me, where Karadzic asks me about a London agreement. I can tell him nothing about it. So now I want to ask the professor, as Mr. Nice used the London agreement and mentioned it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in tab 14, you have a map of the London agreement. As far as I understand this map - it's the original map - this London agreement with its map has nothing to do with Serbia. It's an agreement with Italy to draw Italy into the war on the side of the allies, giving to Italy parts of Dalmatia and so on. It would be useful if you could either confirm or challenge this. It's in tab 14. That's where you have a map of the London agreement. This has nothing to do with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two maps, in actual fact. One is the map drawn in April 1915, when the London agreement was signed, about Italy joining the entente, and it drew in what it would receive as a prize. And in that series of rewards, we see Dalmatia up to the town of Sibenik, the whole of Istria, Trieste, Trentino, part of the Tirol, the Adriatic islands, and a part of Albanian territory as reward given to Italy. The second map is the map that was offered up to Serbia to make amends for the fact that they would lose the Croats, because the Serbs counted upon them as a nation, as an ethnic group, and what they would lose in Dalmatia they would -- and in Macedonia, they would pick this up on the other side. And that is the second map that is relevant here. The first map is not relevant for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this London one with Italy is not the relevant map; is that it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about this other map and focusing on the second map?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we've finished that line of questioning. Now, tell me this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We were looking at tab 15 -- tab 14. You're referring now to another map focusing on -- say the second map. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where the second map is. The map provided here is the London agreement map, and it was not the map and agreement or treaty referring to the issue of Serbia, the question of Serbia. It deals with the relationship between the big powers and Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if we actually have this second map in our exhibits, Professor.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't, but I brought it with me. It has been translated or the comments and legend has been translated into English, and there is a book of maps, a collection of maps. I didn't think we would be discussing this subject, but I have brought it with me. So I would be happy to show the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we place it on the overhead projector, please, map number 2.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just make a moment to find it, please. This is the first map. And that's what was given Italy, or offered to Italy. Now, what was offered to us -- or, rather, to Serbia, I will find that in just a moment. From this collection of maps and books, it is a collection of 28 maps. So here we have the London treaty map, and this is the second map. And this is what they considered Serbia could be given. This was promised to Serbia in London in 1915. It's a rather big map. I don't know if it can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it on the ELMO. What is the point about this map now, Mr. Milosevic? What is the question you want to put to the witness concerning this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you asked to see the second map. I explained what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think the Chamber asked to see the second map. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be that as it may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the territories and what territories were proposed at the time. You mentioned Edward Grey and Clemenceau and others.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was it that Serbia was being offered as an alternative to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was offered was Bosnia, Eastern Slavonia, Backa, Srem, and part of Dalmatia a little more north from Split to the Planck peninsula [phoen]. So a considerable amount of territory, more than Serbia ever considered to be rightfully its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We've dealt with that map now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have dealt with the point that you said was raised by the Prosecution concerning an intercepted conversation with Karadzic in which the London agreement was mentioned. Let us move forward now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, we have now established this. Serbia did not accept this offer, but it decided to go ahead and liberate the Slovenes and Croats and Serbs under Austro-Hungary and the creation of Yugoslavia, in which, as Pasic said, and we quoted him, in which he claims that he -- it must not even have the desire to be dominant. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear to me, and I hope we have clarified it to the Trial Chamber. Serbia did not accept the offer of a Greater Serbia but followed its war goals defined in the Nis declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what do you deduce from the fact that the offer of a Greater Serbia was made by the big powers and that Serbia rejected it? What do you have to say to that? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a sign of its principles, the principles it had fought for from the first uprising to the present day, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now tell me this: What was the general mood of the population at the time in Vojvodina, Baranja, Bosnia, Herzegovina, Slavonia, Dalmatia, that is to say all those regions which were offered to Serbia to expand and enlarge its territory?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year we're talking about, 1915, the population could not -- had no means of expressing its moods, because it was under pressure from war, from a state of emergency, from persecution and so on that you couldn't judge and tap the mood. But once Austria had entered into a crisis in 1918, we saw the burgeoning, true eruption of a wave of enthusiasm for becoming liberated from Austria and for creating a common state, a joint state. And this can be established, first of all, for the public that voiced its mood. One couldn't go from village to village. And except in Vojvodina, unfortunately, the free elections took place there, but otherwise they were not held throughout. But free elections for the Assembly to decide upon the future of the territory. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond What happened was that the Croatian Sabor, in the name of all the South Slavs west of the Drina, made a decision to set up a National Council of the State of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, do you know of a statement made by a Croatian representative in the National Assembly of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, Dr. Ante Pavlovic, and he just happens to have the same name as the latter-day Ante Pavelic of the Independent State of Croatia, but do you know of a statement of his about the dilemma that they faced as to what they should do? And what was their dilemma in actual -- actually, the dilemma of the Croatian political elite, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dilemma arose in 1917, first, whether they should see the unification of South Slav lands under the Habsburg Monarchy, and in that connection the May declaration was passed with the representatives of the Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes in the Austrian parliament, in the Austrian delegations, or not to accept this solution and to unite with Serbia. The situation became quite clear in the broadest political circles in 1918, and that was that a unification with Serbia should be chosen. There was to be a dilemma right up to the disintegration of Yugoslavia, whether it should be a centralist state or a federal state, federal kingdom with a federal system. However, that dilemma was to destroy the Yugoslav entity between the two world wars, because no solution was found, it was only intimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, right. Now, this option on the part of the Kingdom of Serbia and the Serb people to set up Yugoslavia as a country, was it the best possible proof of the fact that Austrian -- Austro-Hungarian propaganda about the bogeyman of Serbia and later on, was that a false propaganda?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was false, because I said a moment ago that the only true real idea of a Greater Serbia was actually born in 1915 and not among Serb circles because the Serb government at the time was still on its own territory in the town of Nis, so not in Serb circles but amongst the circles of the big powers, the entente powers on whose side Serbia fought. So any propaganda along those lines was false propaganda unless we have in mind the individual instances, marginal instances that we mentioned a moment ago, and transitory cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am concerned to ensure that we are making the best use of the time available to us. As I said before, I think it's -- it's open to you, I think you're entitled to refute, to try to refute this concept of a Greater Serbia since it was an important part of the Prosecution's case, and I understand that you're doing this by tracing the history of Serbia to show that at no time in that history was this concept prevalent. Now, you have dealt with the First World War. Can we then move on to the period between the First and the Second World War -- just the high points in that year, and then you move on to the Second World War, and then the era from the Second World War to the present time. Otherwise, we are in danger of being drowned in a sea of historical detail which is not -- not necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We just want the broad outline of what you're trying to do, and which, as I've said, you have a right to do, in my view at any rate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've gained a general impression and general picture. Now we'll look at how this myth of a Greater Serbia -- or, rather, we're going to pass through its dynamics and the dynamics it followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, the Serb people, did it support the survival of Yugoslavia during World War II?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was this Yugoslav programme that mobilised the national liberation forces in the whole of Yugoslavia, throughout Yugoslavia, and of course among the Serbs. And 80 per cent, right up until the end of 1943, in fact, and the beginning of 1944, 80 per cent of the fighters in the national liberation army for the national liberation war were Serbs who had opted for the Yugoslav solution, which was offered up at that time by the Communist Party, which was the leader of the national liberation war. The Serbian people rejected, did not respond to the other kinds of Greater Serbian designs offered up by -- in declarative terms by the liberation movement of Draza Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the Serb people supported the survival of Yugoslavia during World War II. Did it do so as well in the 1990s, of the 20th century? Did it lend its support and came out in support of Yugoslavia's survival?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there's any doubt about that. The Serbs, both in Serbia and especially the Serbs outside Serb, living in Bosnia, for example, and Croatia, were convinced, and that's a fact, that it is only in Yugoslavia that they could remain rallied in a single country within Yugoslavia's borders. If Yugoslavia were to fall apart, were to disintegrate, they would go back to the situation they were in in 1918. That is to say they would go back to other people's countries, alien countries, alien borders, even like in Bosnia where they were the relative majority. And that is why the Serbs were Yugoslav oriented in the majority. And they were ready to defend that Yugoslavia, some of them by taking up arms, as in Krajina and the people in Bosnia, and others working in propaganda, giving material aid and assistance and in ways of that kind. So in the 1990s, the beginning of the 1990s, it was Yugoslavia that was being defended and the survival of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you mentioned how many casualties there were in World War I. Now, can you tell us, if this won't take away too much time, could you just take a look at those facts and figures, and can we say how many Serb casualties there were in both the world wars and in that process of creation and preservation of Yugoslavia both in World War I and World War II?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can show the Court a map which was drawn and compiled by the American intelligence service at the end of 1942 and which is based on very secure data that were kept highly secret and confidential. It was the intelligence service which was to give birth to the CIA later on, led by William Donovan, and it compiled a map of Serb casualties, Serb victims in Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia and Vojvodina, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the relevance of Serb casualties in the two world wars to the exercise that, as I said, you are now legitimately involved in, that is, debunking this idea of a Greater Serbia? What is the relevance of this to that exercise, the fact that Serbia suffered casualties in the two world wars? How does that serve to contradict the idea of a Greater Serbia? Because if you can't explain, I'm not going to allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain it, Mr. Robinson. Don't you worry about that. I wanted to hear from the professor, and I don't know whether it's been properly translated, interpreted, because you mentioned between the two world wars, how many casualties the Serb people gave to have Yugoslavia survive and persevere. The amount of lives it laid down for the creation and preservation of Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia. Bear in mind every word that I say -- I think of every word I say before I say it. So how many lives the Serb people laid down for the creation and preservation and survival of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. I have to rule on it. Mr. Milosevic has to await my ruling, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It's marginally relevant since it bears on the question of the creation and preservation of Yugoslavia. A short answer, though, Professor, a short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The total number of losses, in the briefest possible terms, according to existing facts and figures of Serbia Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond and the Serbs, the Serb people, the -- in the two world wars, were approximately 2.5 million people. That's the shortest answer I can give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, well, we are now at the time for the break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how much longer do you plan to be with this witness for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters heard only the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The microphone is on now. I'll do my best to finish the examination-in-chief by the middle of this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, a few moments ago you explained how much was invested in creating Yugoslavia and ensuring its survival, and before that you also said what Serbia brought into this new joint state. Now I wish to put a question to you as to an historian. If a people invests millions of human lives into the creation and survival of a state, invests its statehood, its international legal subjectivity, et cetera, what seems more normal and more natural to you and more probable; that that people will try to preserve the state for which it had sacrificed so much or that it will do its to break it up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not a proper question. It will call for an answer that is just too opinionated. It's not relying on the professor's historical skills and knowledge. I think you should ask another question. You can use that in your address, in your closing address, but it's not appropriate as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the 1990s, did the Serb people try to preserve Yugoslavia into which they had invested such a great deal or did they turn to projects that were rejected by history?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they addressed themselves to the state that they had created themselves, and the Serbian people had terrible negative experience from the First World War and the Second World War inflicted on them by the forces that in the 1990s proclaimed secession and called for the break-up of Yugoslavia. So it is quite clear why Serbs took that side and why they opted for preserving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these rejected projects, you refer to them too. There were such projects. You have tabs 6 onwards. This is a few maps. There are a few maps here. For example, in tab 6. If you wish to have a look at that, this is homogenous Serbia, and the title is "Dr. Stevan Moljevic, attorney-at-law from Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was this map?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this infernal terror that the Serb people was subjected to in the Krajinas, in Bosnia, in Herzegovina by the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia in 1941, the lawyer Moljevic left Banja Luka and was in the town of Niksic in Montenegro, and he was thinking about the break-up of Yugoslavia and the creation of a Greater Serbia, and he made this map which was sent to Draza Mihajlovic's headquarters. There was a map there already of the Belgrade headquarters, and Draza Mihajlovic compared the two maps, and he preferred Moljevic's map. When Moljevic reached, in March 1942, Draza Mihajlovic's headquarters, that's when this map was adopted. There was a countless number of maps. The Chetnik movement was an incoherent movement, and there were lots of maps and lots of ideas bandied about, but the objective of Draza Mihajlovic's movement were these ideas of Stevan Moljevic. They were in force until January 1944 when they were modified. Moljevic envisaged a Greater Serbia, even bigger than the one that was offered by the London treaty. The London offer, rather than the London treaty. And Moljevic envisaged that this should be a homogenous Serbia from a national point of view along the following lines: The non-Serb population will be allowed to leave on their own or will be exchanged for those Serbs which remain outside this Greater Serbia. This programme was rejected by the Chetniks themselves. It was revised at the so-called Sveti Sava Congress in the village of Bar in January 1944 when, under pressure exerted by the Allies and because of the general feeling that prevailed among the Allies, a decision was made to create a federative Yugoslavia with Serbia at its centre. However, that was not accepted either by the Serb people or, rather, the National Liberation Movement, and all these plans, Moljevic's and of the Sveti Sava Congress, all went down the drain in 1945 when the Chetnik movement was defeated once it openly collaborated with the German occupier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this plan of a Greater Serbia was never the official policy of these leading forces in Yugoslavia or the Yugoslav state or of the Serbian politicians who were in power?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not, and it could never succeed because it envisaged further fierce fighting for territories, and the Serb people actually didn't want this. Therefore, every such project failed and failed not only the examination of history but also of that very moment in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was the creation of a Greater Serbia ever part of any official programme of the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I believe that I know quite a bit, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now let me ask you something else. The building of any kind of greater state, is that something that entails territorial continuity, compactness, et cetera, everything that this state consists of?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. And it is interesting that all the peoples in our neighbourhood had such plans and such wishes, dreams, if you wish. I was astonished when I saw the following. I never would have thought that the Slovenians would want to have that, least of all. They also had the idea of a Greater Slovenia, and I can show you a map of that project, too, but it was not carried through ever because a Greater Serbia or a Greater Croatia or Montenegro or Slovenia simply could not be created in the Balkan religious and national cauldron. The Serb intelligentsia understood that from day one, from the first Serbian uprising in 1804 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You said that this means that there should be a compact territory and there should be continuity in creating such a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think this has some relevance and we need to be precise. You asked him whether the building of any kind of a greater state, whether that entails territorial continuity, compactness, and he said, "For the most part, yes." So I understand him to be saying that the element of territorial contiguity [Realtime transcript read in error "continuity"] is not a necessary element in the concept of a Greater Serbia or a Greater Slovenia. It may be possible to have that concept in the absence of territorial contiguity [Realtime transcript read in error "continuity"]. It doesn't have to exist in all cases. Would you like to clarify that? Please clarify that, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I bore in mind this European plan when between the two world wars there were separated territories of a state, and that is a great misfortune. I'm talking about Poland. There was that corridor which divided Poland into two, and that was a source of constant disputes between Germany and Poland. Therefore, such cases are possible and have existed in history, but most people try to avoid it. If you wish, we have the example of the two Chinas today. It is one state so it does not have continuity but with two regimes and two territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whereas the transcript has me saying "territorial continuity," I said territorial contiguity, which, in my view, is a better description of the idea. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, I understood what you were saying in the following way; that the creation of any kind of greater state means that there is territorial contiguity.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please place this map on the overhead projector now. This is the Cutileiro plan map for Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have it, but I have prepared it here so that we could show it. Then I will put a question to the professor. Could you please place it on the overhead projector. This is the Cutileiro map, or, rather, the map that was called the Cutileiro plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this map, Professor. This is the map that on the 18th of March, 1992, all three sides signed. According to this map, Bosnia-Herzegovina was cantonised. It was an independent state, but it consisted of cantons. According to this plan, is there territorial continuity between Serb territories? You can see very nicely what the Serbian part is with horizontal lines, then the Croatian part are dark areas, and the Muslim part is white, and Sarajevo has slanted lines.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously there is no continuity. And if one means a Greater Serbia, if that is what is attempted, this would not be the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. That's what I'm asking you. Does this kind of map and this kind of project fit into a concept of a Greater Serbia even if it did exist?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any serious person could think that this is the road leading to a Greater Serbia and that nobody could have counted on creating a Greater Serbia in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted this plan before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not explored this, but as a private person, I have information from the media, and I know that the Serbs accepted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 25th of March, 1992, Izetbegovic withdrew his signature of acceptance?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, he accepted it first and then he withdrew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He signed it on the 18th and then withdrew it on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this kind of map and this kind of plan certainly could not fit into any kind of concept of a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that we from Serbia, and I personally, gave support to this position taken by the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs and their acceptance of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an historian, does it seem possible to you that someone is planning the creation a Greater Serbia and at the same time accepting and supporting a plan that means a completely different thing? Does history know of such absurd examples?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say anything but confirm what you've just said, that history practically does not know of any such absurd examples. Of course, I cannot remember all of world history right now but perhaps there were such cases somewhere but not in Balkan history and not in Serbian history, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the map of the Vance-Owen Plan now from 1993, the spring of 1993. It also envisages --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It also envisages an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina divided into cantons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do we have that kind of map also? Have you offered that map to the Chamber or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't submitted it to the Chamber. I thought that all these maps of the Cutileiro Plan and Vance-Owen Plan are in existence here. It is not being challenged by anyone that these are documents that were part of an international conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- the accused has got to comply with our practices, and if he's going to produce an exhibit that's already an exhibit, he should really give the Registry and the Court advance notice, A, to ensure that it is an exhibit; and B, to ensure that it's the same version of the document that's already in evidence. I can't assist at the moment as to the question whether either of these documents is an exhibit or not. We may be able to in a minute or so but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, was this map exhibited by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. I believe so, because the Vance-Owen Plan was referred to several times here, and it would have been impossible not to have admitted the map. The professor knows this map very well, too, the map related to the Vance-Owen Plan. My question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not like that. Not like that. Let us deal with this point. You must comply with the practices and the procedures of the Court. Mr. Nice has made a point, following upon Judge Kwon's perfectly proper question to you. The map is not before the Chamber. We have been through this before. We are repeating ourselves, Mr. Milosevic, and I warn you that if I make the determination that these things are happening because you do not care about the procedure, I will not allow you to produce the evidence. If I am not satisfied that you are making a good faith effort to comply with the procedures, you will not be allowed to adduce the evidence. We have procedures here and they must be complied with. Let the professor comment on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Vance-Owen map, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What was the question you were asking? Let Mr. Milosevic ask the question. I think that's where we broke off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is the same as it was for the Cutileiro map. This map and this plan, can they fit into any kind of idea or concept of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never did. As far as I can remember from my knowledge of what happens in public affairs, this was one of the chances to stop the war in Bosnia rather than create a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you do know that Prime Minister Mitsotakis of Greece and President Cosic of Yugoslavia and I were in Pale then when this plan was discussed, and it is a well-known fact that we supported the plan. So as an historian, does it seem possible to you that somebody plans to create a Greater Serbia and at the same time accepts and supports plans that mean something completely different, that is quite the opposite, as can be seen from here?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This session took place at Pale, and I followed this from my hospital bed. The night -- the session went on all night, and in the morning I heard your statement and Mr. Cosic's statement, and you gave your full support to this plan. I don't think that anybody could have this kind of ulterior motive to say do it and then to go back on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I allowed that question to pass, but as with another question of a similar kind, that's a comment which is appropriate for your address.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is so obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's so obvious -- you make it in your address. The witness can't take the matter any further by answering a question of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's make a small digression now, because I think it's important to say this -- or, rather, I'm interested in your answer.
