In the policies of the Serbian political ideologues, during the 19th and 20th centuries, were there any Greater Serbian ideas and actions, and what were their results? We have touched upon Moljevic and some other examples. Are you aware of any other exponents of such ideas and what the results of their ideas were?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no serious politicians with such ideas. Such ideas did emerge from time to time in public life, denying the existence, for example, of Macedonians as a nation or demands that Serb lands be established and that negotiations with other nations be conducted from positions of power. There was a paper called Srpski Glas published by the Serb Cultural Club just before World War II, which published such ideas, but the then-government banned this paper. I have no knowledge of any other examples of prominent politicians. As far as Slobodan Jovanovic goes, I've studied his writings and I can find no trace of such ideas. He was concerned with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just help with the plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have sight at the moment of the Cutileiro Plan offered just now, but the accused should have known that it was he who'd put the Cutileiro Plan in as D209, I think, and I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich, as ever, for her rapid retrieval of this detail. Whether it's the same version of the plan or not, I'm not sure, because I haven't got it on the screen at the moment. The Vance-Owen Plan is, we understand, Exhibit 396, tab 10. Again, without being able to see the maps and compare them, I can't know if they're the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice, for that assistance, which should have been provided by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. If this question refers to any map of the Vance-Owen Plan, I accept that, because it's common knowledge what the Vance-Owen Plan looked like. We are talking about areas from which the army of the Bosnian Serbs was to withdraw and areas from which the army of BH and the Bosnian Croats was supposed to withdraw. That's the area around Sarajevo. But any map exhibited here would refer to the same issue. So I accept any map exhibited here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the Republic of Serbia proper - I am referring to the years between 1991 and 1999 - were there any phenomena showing Greater Serbian tendencies, aggressive behaviour, destructive behaviour, hegemony, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that -- I think there must be some limit to the degree to which the witness can be invited to trespass on the territory of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to ask another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about Greater Serbia hegemonism emerging in Serbia in the last decades of the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was rhetorical and propaganda made advocating these ideas. For example, the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Renewal Movement. They did not, however, advocate a war for the expansion of Serbia. They were simply giving verbal support to the Serb people and the desire of those people in the Krajina and in Bosnia to remain in a community with Serbia. I cannot say that these were coherent Greater Serbia plans, but even when such ideas did emerge in pre-election rallies and speeches, they were very effectively suppressed by the then-authorities; by your government and by the parliament of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when examining your colleagues, Professor Avramov and the academician Mihajlo Markovic, Mr. Nice - and I've only found it on the transcript today - this is page 32501 in the case of Professor Avramov and 33550 in the case of Professor Markovic, referred to the writings published in a magazine called Epoha. You have copies of this magazine and so do I. This was raised here as an important issue. Therefore, I wish to ask you to assist us by clarifying certain points. For example, on line 6 it says there was a magazine called Epoha published for a couple of years, "[In English] in 1991, and it was effectively the magazine of the accused's SPS party; correct?" [Interpretation] This was the question put by Mr. Nice to Smilja Avramov, who said she was unable to answer his question because she wasn't aware of that. As for Mihajlo Markovic, you are aware of a magazine called Epoha, and so on and so forth. He couldn't say precisely what this was about. However, as we have obtained copies of this magazine in the meantime, and Mr. Nice has exhibited them, you are aware, Professor, that this magazine was issued in the 1990s. This is the issue exhibited here. It's the first issue, of the 22nd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit, Mr. Milosevic, that I was not aware of the existence of such a magazine. However, I heard about it for the first time when following the proceedings and the testimony of witnesses Avramov and Markovic. And then I made an effort. I asked a young colleague of mine to find this issue for me, and he did. I looked at it, and nowhere could I see that this was a magazine of the Socialist Party. I am a member of the Socialist Party and have been since it was founded. I have to admit I don't read the weekly press because it's a huge waste of time; however, I did not even know that this magazine existed. Later on, I found that among the people writing in this magazine there were current and former members of the Socialist Party, but I also noticed something else. In the back, this is published by a limited liability company, and you have commercial advertisements here. This is an institute for international management, Suhcesije, European Council of Management, and a number of other such organisations, and they started this magazine, as far as I can tell, and they managed to get some prominent journalists and scholars to write in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that organisation, the -- what is it, the European Council that you referred to that publish the magazine? Where is it based? From -- does it say on the magazine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was based in Belgrade. It says so in the magazine. As far as I know, a certain Mr. Zecevic established it. His name is Milja Zecevic, if I'm correct. He founded this international management centre, and he had a branch office in Paris. Later on, as far as I can recall but I'm not absolutely sure, he moved to Los Angeles in the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the people publishing advertisements here were not the publishers of Epoha. In the impression on page 1, it says published by Epoha Limited, Company Limited. Is this correct? Not by the Socialist Party but by Epoha Company Limited.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people publishing advertisements here are neither the publishers nor of a -- the owners of this magazine.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they're certainly financing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As this refers to October 1991, from the magazine which we have finally obtained, for example, here you can see the biggest building construction company building flats, and they're advertising their properties and so on, there's a lot of advertising here, but the fundamental question as to whether this -- this is a magazine of the Socialist Party, the answer is no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the content of the magazine goes, have you managed to read it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem to you that there are various opinions expressed here, many of which are contradictory, and this is a part of the freedom of speech and journalism which was prevalent in early 1991, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: More leading questions, speeches, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have just asked a question which tells the witness what the answer is. We have discussed this before, that you are not allowed to ask leading questions. Rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popov, I assume you are aware that there were many polemics and discussions current at the time about various maps and that the various newspapers and magazines were flooded with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In that situation, everybody speculated. There's a famous character in literature who, even in difficult situations, attempted to promote himself. His name was Ostap Bender. So there were various plans current at the time. I saw that some of them came from eminent people, but I have to say, and it's my fault, I don't know who the people putting forward maps in this magazine are, I assume they're not very prominent people in public life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, various writers express various opinions here, is that clear from this issue of Epoha?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it last night because I brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 15, for example. I don't know who this Dr. Jovan Ilic is. Maybe you know him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that he is a demographer of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, a demographer. Well, look on page 15. I will quote point 1. He says, "It is our opinion that the frequently mentioned border, the western border of Karlovac-Virovitica-Karlobag of the Serbs lands, map number 1, is not favourable to the solution of the Serbian issue." And, well, now you say he was a demographer. Because many Croats would then remain in the third Yugoslavia, about a million and a half of them. Later, from 1981, he was probably looking at statistics, the census from the current Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have this exhibit, as far as I know, unless it's one of the tabs that I've not tracked down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 786 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, but I'm not sure. There's a colour version that we have here and we only have a black and white version, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice exhibited this issue of Epoha. I'm using his exhibit. I don't know what his number for it is, but I know that Mihajlo Markovic was mentioned and that this was exhibited as if it were something important. I'm trying to show here that this is a pure manipulation on the part of Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The magazine to which you're referring is the same magazine, Mr. Milosevic, that Mr. Nice exhibited? Is it the same issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Yes, it is. It's the identical issue. I assume that my copy has more pages because Mr. Nice has extracted a map which he has adduced with this issue of Epoha, but the magazine deals with all sorts of various issues. It was simply one among a number of magazines published at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 786.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I've now got 786, and indeed it does appear that there is more in this exhibit than we had, because we only had as much as we had. Again, the accused has got to make exhibits available if they are to be dealt with. Perhaps the Chamber would also, if it thinks it should or can, deal with the entirely inappropriate terminology of the accused in referring to my conduct of this case. As the Court knows, I've been very tolerant of his bad use of language, but the word "manipulation" is inappropriate and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he did use that word, yes, then it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Line 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, that is not acceptable language here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will quote another passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you continue, you should have copies of this magazine for the benefit of the Chamber and the Prosecution so that we can follow it. Your examination-in-chief is not a private dialogue between yourself and the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, Mr. Robinson, you're holding a copy of the magazine in your hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I managed to secure this after the efforts of the -- calling upon the efforts of Judge Kwon and the Deputy Registrar. You are to produce it. That's your job. When you organise your case overnight, you must make sure that you come to court with copies of the exhibits or the documents on which you're going to rely in your examination-in-chief. The next time it happens, I will not allow it. I'm not going to allow you to lead the evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you through with this magazine now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not. I wanted to put a few more questions to the Professor. I wanted to quote from page 20, because you can see a wide range of viewpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have page 20. The two last passages in the last column, it says: "People, especially young people, should be brought up to respect their own ethnic and national characteristics in the spirit of general geoglobalism, democratic Europeanism, and the spirit of modern, cultural, scientific, scholarly and other processes. Young people must be educated to respect the equality of citizens in their own country and in the world. We have to avoid the situation which emerged after the collapse of communist one-mindedness. Unfortunately, it has been replaced by nationalist one-mindedness. This means that we have to develop further the process of democratisation." There are various ideas here, critical views of the events that transpired in 1991. Does what you are holding in your hands now, is it different from the general kind of articles published at the time? Is there any Greater Serbian chauvinist ideology imparted in this magazine published by a company limited, as we can see, and not the Socialist Party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the quotation you read out I have marked myself as a sort of evidence or proof of a healthy political way of thinking and healthy thought, which in the mad times of nationalist and chauvinist aspirations generally was something that was heard. Now, I don't know who this man Dr. Ilic is, but with these variants set out, I don't know whether I can agree with his variants but I do agree with what you just said, because this is the voice of reason, that the youth, internationalist youth, if you want to put it that way, should be educated in a tolerant manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that while The Hague Conference was still going on and well in political and scientific circles were discussing different borders, administrative borders, non-administrative borders, and so on and so forth, that it was already quite clear that Slovenia's and Croatia's secession was imminent already at that time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is October 1991, isn't it? And Slovenia proclaimed its secession in June, if I'm correct. Of course, I didn't think I'd be answering questions of this nature, but I think Croatia did so a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who imposed the fact that the question of borders should be put on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were stepping down, who were seceding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Armed secession took place and a general discussion of borders began; is that right? At scientific forums, laymen's forums, expert meetings; everywhere, in fact?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it began with an attack on the Yugoslav People's Army, a strong attack on the army and the killing of unarmed soldiers and the blocking of barracks, and so on and so forth. And immediately after that came the question of borders. That was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, with this particular author, Mr. Rakic, we can see that the author considers that it is Europe who should settle the issue of borders.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, that's how it turned out, and that's what it would appear, because the man -- this man looked at the realistic situation, and he thought that the influence of the international factor was so great on our internal affairs that that would be the right way to go about it and that one couldn't avoid that influence. So that is how I understand the suggestion on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I won't dwell on this any more, but as you have read through this magazine, is it clear that it collides with the idea of a Greater Serbia as well?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear, because nobody is striving for a Greater Serbia anywhere, not this man Rakic and not the man Ilic either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again that's an entirely leading, extremely tendentious question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think in the circumstances we'll allow it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the professor has already answered anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are in danger of beating this point to death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will refrain from beating this topic to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you quote examples of certain Serbian politicians in the 1990s, perhaps, who advocated an aggressive presence, the establishment of paramilitary units or anything of that kind, any similar things from Serbia vis-a-vis or towards other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the first military formation or, rather, paramilitary formation that was set up. That was sometime in mid-1991. I myself live in the city of Novi Sad, which is across from the Danube with the fortress of Petrov Varadin. It is a large fortress with exercise grounds, training grounds, and that's where training took place of the so-called Serbian Guard. And the television televised that and the first commander who was to die in Krajina later on, his name was Djordje Bozovic, nicknamed Giska, explained how they were undergoing training and that they were preparing to go to defend the Serb people, because allegedly this was something that was not being done by the Serbian government in sufficient measure or, rather, the Yugoslav government, as it was still during that time. So this was a formation, a unit which was established by the Party of the Serbian revival movement -- renewal movement, and the leader is Vuk Draskovic. So the Serbian Renewal Movement with Vuk Draskovic at its head. Later on I read that a man named Arkan, who was killed in the year 2000, followed suit, and we heard of some Seselj's volunteers. I don't think that was a paramilitary formation. He went around making a lot of noise, holding patriotic speeches and so on and so forth. It was more a verbal form of agitation to suppress the patriotic spirit and that his men went to the Yugoslav army as volunteers. That's all I know, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this Serbian guard of Vuk Draskovic's that you mentioned, what was its relationship towards the state and the state institutions and me personally as the Serbian Renewal Movement of Vuk Draskovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the renewal movement went to the -- led up to the demonstrations in Belgrade in 1990, the destructive ones. Then he set up a guard which I read somewhere numbered 800 men somewhere in Lika. That's where they went to fight. And this man Giska, I might be wrong on this score and I do apologise if I am, but it seems to me that that man Giska said at the time that they could -- they were capable of mobilising 7.000 men at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But my question was what was the relationship between the Serbian Renewal Movement and Serbian Guard towards the official powers that be in Serbia and Yugoslavia of the day?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the extreme opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In 1990, the Party of Democratic Action of Alija Izetbegovic formed its branch in Serbia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that was in the region called Sandzak. Sulejman Ugljanin led that particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll remember the large-scale rallies.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember them well. And I remember one particular rally at which that man held a speech precisely against the rallying of Muslims in Sandzak and linking themselves up to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Party of Democratic Action of Alija Izetbegovic who were in Sandzak, that party. But you remember Draskovic's rallies too?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Draskovic's rallies, and I remember on one occasion Ugljanin, for example, made a lot of noise and shouted and said that Serbia didn't ask them about anything and that's why they will seek recourse and protection from Alija Izetbegovic or, rather, the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you remember about Draskovic's rally?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he launched threats and said that anybody carrying green flags and from the Party of Democratic Action would come under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Socialist Party of Serbia? Did it establish its branch in Bosnia-Herzegovina or any other republic apart from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it did. I don't know about that, and as a party member, I would have to know, but I don't know anything about that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the authorities, because there were the demonstrations by Ugljanin on one side and Draskovic on the other, that there was a media campaign to quell the unrest amongst the population in Sandzak at the time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read just two papers and I read two papers, I've been reading them for 15 years, and I watch television, of course, and I listen to the radio, and what I remember is this: That the Socialist Party always launched appeals to calm the situation down, advocating tolerant relations, democratic action, and so on and so forth. So I cannot state that there were any, absolutely none, no warmongering policies among the Socialist Party itself at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, Professor: You're an eyewitness of all the events that took place in the last decade of the 20th century and of course the times that went by previously and you're an historian also. Did you ever note in Serbia any relationship of discrimination during the wars in Bosnia and Croatia, either towards the Croats or towards the Muslims or towards the Hungarians or towards anyone else, any other ethnic group for that matter?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I myself live in Vojvodina province, for example, and there are 20 ethnic groups - 23, to be exact - living there, speaking six languages. We speak six languages in Vojvodina and communicate in six languages. Papers and magazines are published in six languages as are television broadcasts, radio broadcasts, and so on. So I have to say that during that period of time, there was absolutely no -- except for the unfortunate case that it seems to be mentioned time and again, that incident at Hrtkovci -- I cannot remember a single other instance or case, either talking to my colleagues, friends, associates who were Croats, Hungarians, or anything else. Our relationships have remained good. They have not been upset from either side. And I think that the policy waged by the Socialist Party in the Republic of Serbia first and foremost was a policy of tolerance which accepted even Muslim refugees, for example, coming in from Bosnia. And we were all witnesses to that. We knew all about that. And I would go to Mount Slativo, for example, where this was the topic of the day. So I cannot accept any accusations made against Serbia that Serbia waged any kind of discriminatory policy towards anybody. People did say, for example -- Hungarians did say, or Hungarian nationalists used to say that a lot of young people left Serbia at the time. Well, yes, they did. They left to avoid having to join up, to join the army. So there were people fleeing in that way. But anybody else fleeing because of discrimination and threats, I don't know any instance of that kind, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Vojvodina you would have been well placed to see that had it taken place.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the famous Hrtkovci that are mentioned all the time. Are you aware of the fact that the perpetrators of that incident were arrested?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the papers wrote about these people being arrested, that some people were arrested, and unless I'm mistaken, I know Mrs. Margit Savovic, she was on a special mission there to ascertain what had actually happened. And I heard this from her when she visited the Matica Srpska organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I just have a few more questions for you. You know full well about the situation in the northern part of Serbia and Vojvodina province, and you yourself said that there was no discrimination there. Can you tell us, but just in a few words, please, give your comments about the position of the Serbs and Croats in Hungary, for example, if you were to compare some years. Let's take, for example, the Trianon agreement, for example, and the present times. According to my facts and figures, there were 150.000 Croats in Hungary at the time. Now there are only 13.000. There were over 30.000 Serbs there, now there are only 3.500 Serbs in Hungary. And at that time in Serbia we had 300.000 Hungarians living in Yugoslavia and we still have 300.000 Hungarians living in Yugoslavia. Are those facts and figures correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct, and I was a member of an inter-academy study group. We spent 10 days touring South Slav minorities in Hungary, for example. This was in 1988. Antun Vratusa was the head of the delegation, the head of the study group going to Hungary, and we visited a large number of institutions and, amongst others, the ministry in charge of that question, and so those facts and figures are almost identical to the figures quoted by the ministry, by representatives of that particular ministry. They said that there were at least 10.000 Serbs but that they didn't wish to declare themselves as Serbs, and that there are still at least 30.000 Croats who did not wish to declare themselves as Croats because they have had some very difficult experience in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many Croats were living in Hungary earlier, during the Trianon agreement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, approximately, in countries -- Hungarians in countries belonging to Yugoslavia there was a slightly larger figure, but there was a considerable number of South Slavs who stayed on, remained living in Hungary. And according to the Trianon agreement, the possibility was given for an option. People could decide whether they wished to move and resettle or not. There was some resettlement but the results were not impressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, move on to another area of questioning, because the relevance of this area is questionable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. I won't take up more of the professor's time. All I would like to do is to ask him to comment on a couple of maps that we have provided here among the exhibits. And I have in mind map 13 -- or, rather, tab 13 and tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So just in the briefest possible terms, Professor, could you comment upon Greater Albania, tab 13, tab 15, and tab 16.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are self-explanatory maps, and I'm just going to make one small comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the maps placed -- at least one of the maps placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have a map of the Prizren League, for example. The Prizren League was founded in 1878. It was the first Greater Albania movement, and I have to say that not a single Balkan people, Balkan nations in their national aspirations were so consistent as were the Albanians. Their plans for a Greater Albania dating back to 1878 and in later years, and we have three of them here, from the times of the Italian occupation, from the year 2001, they are almost identical. There are very few deviations. So this Greater Albania comprises the western reaches of Serbia, Western Macedonia, and western parts of Greece, the so-called Camorija area. And you'll find this identical situation in all the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to deal with a small matter of detail. You will be provided with a selection of prints from the magazine Epoha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A section of prints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's parts of various copies of Epoha --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The transcript has you as saying a selection of principles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the magazine itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will distribute this exhibit and explain it to the Court and then I'm only going to ask you to look at one point, Professor, so don't be too troubled.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not troubled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we have in the first, if you look at it - I don't know if you read English - you'll see in the first few pages typewritten versions of the entries in various copies of Epoha. See, the first page is a typewritten version of what appears on the printing detail for the 22nd of October; the second page has, in both Serbian and in English beside it, the entries for the printing of the 29th of October; and then we come to the next page, which is the 26th of December; and then the 16th of December. Over the page we come to the 11th of June, and the 13th of August. Now, the intention was that the relevant material should always have been translated into English where appropriate. It hasn't happened, but you can help us. If you go now, please, to the second to last page of this little selection of documents. And if the usher would be good enough to display one on the overhead projector if you've got a spare of that. Second to last page. You'll see a page from Epoha. It looks like that. Yes, please. Epoha from the 11th of June, 2002. We can see that date at the top, right-hand corner. But if you put the document, please, Usher, so we can see the bottom, right-hand corner of the page. Right at the bottom. No, right at the bottom. Further down. Right at the bottom. Further down. There it is. That's it. Now, what we see there on the right-hand side is a passage --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Nice is talking about 2002 now, and all the maps he talked about pertained to 1991 and the magazine from 1991. Now he is trying to prove something through the year 2002; who published the magazine and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we don't know yet what Mr. Nice is trying to prove. Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the English-Serbian version of this, which is earlier on, didn't translate the word Osnivac, so can you just read out the first line of the printing details beside "Epoha," beginning with Osnivac.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, yes. Yes. It says: "Founder, Socialist Party of Serbia. Publisher, the company Medijas. Director and editor-in-chief, Milorad Vujovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the next page and look at the same part of it for the 13th of August of 2002, just to be fair and to see what is involved, we now see that Osnivac has changed, and can you read the first line, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Founder, the Medijas company. Publisher, the Medijas company. Address, Studentski Trg 15, Belgrade. Director, Milorad Vujovic", et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, with why this June edition, June 2002, refers to the founder being the Serbian Socialist Party? Can you help us with that, since you've given an opinion on the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat that this is the first time I see this magazine, so I can hardly help you with this, how come it says the Socialist Party of Serbia. If the founder was the Socialist Party of Serbia, then I was not a very good member, because I did not follow the party newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now come to your report, and perhaps you'd be good enough, please, to help me with a couple of general points. You're an academic, and you're used, I take it, to preparing academic papers; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Academic papers are for reading by fellow academics and people of intelligence and learning, and they have to justify the conclusions that they reach. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's just take one tiny example of the evidence that you've given and I think that you've referred to in your report, the reference to "axes in their heads." Do you remember giving us evidence about how people were killed with axes in their heads?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. I do remember very well. I remember the document very well. No, they were not actually killed, but this was what was being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we were to look through your report, could you tell me where I could find the source for that little detail?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. It is in the two volumes entitled "Material about Serbs in Croatia," published by Vasilije Krestic, an historian, four or five years ago. In these two volumes, there are about 800 documents. One of these documents is a note of Isa Krsnjavi, a writer and active supporter of the Party of Rights, who visited Ban Cuvaj and suggested that the Serb issue be resolved radically. In response to Cuvaj's question how it can be resolved radically, he said, "By taking an axe to their heads." And then the other man said, Well, you cannot kill 800.000 people. That's what the source says. This is an original source that Krestic published --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Professor Popov, can you show me -- it may well be that I've missed it, and it will be entirely my mistake if I have, but have you identified that source in your report to this Court?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted my report together with the notes. In these notes, everything was identified. I don't know if you received these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... bibliography extract, but I haven't got --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't seen one footnote or end note in this report. So there's nothing in it that I've ever been able to track. Where are these notes that you say come with it? Maybe they weren't provided. Maybe we've mislaid them. Maybe the Court has got them and I haven't.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here they are. It was probably mislaid somewhere, because I have them here. Straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's something we raised in our filing about this witness, that there were no footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let them be passed first to the Chamber and then to the Prosecutor. Professor Popov, hand over the notes to the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I just add something to what Professor Popov said? I was confident all the time that whenever the professor referred to footnotes or notes or whatever had been made available to everyone, because they're marked in the text, and perhaps this was a technical mistake. They were not typed on the actual pages of the report, they were added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have indicating footnotes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's a technical mistake. I do have these marks in my text, and I have exactly 69 footnotes that he mentioned as sources in this report of his. That's what the professor did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is another example, I'm afraid, of the problems caused by the accused choosing only to take part in procedure when it suits him. Because if he had read the filing -- had he read and responded to the filing of the 18th of October of this year, rather than disregarding it, I imagine, he would have seen that we invited the Chamber to order that the report be rewritten and footnotes or end notes added referencing the sources for the claims made, because we were alarmed at having to deal with an expert report that had no sources at all. And, Your Honour, I don't propose to ask for time to deal with it unless in the course of the break I find something particularly concerning, because I'm not sure of the particular scope and relevance of this report, but it is very unsatisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I make this remark with great care, but you have done a disservice to Professor Popov. You have done him a great disservice, because he produced for you a report which had footnotes, and yet you did not ensure that the report which is before the Chamber is one which replicates those footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know how that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder too. I wonder too. This is not only to the detriment of the expert but it's to my detriment too. What would my motive be not to supply the footnotes along with the report? All the footnotes were given at the end of the report, and this is only to the detriment of our work here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have here the text in Serbian. Can you tell me where I'll find reference to the first footnote? On which page will I find reference to the first footnote?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 1, at the beginning of paragraph 2, after the word "confusion," where there is a full stop, and that is where footnote number 1 is. That's the first footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no sign of it on the copy which I have here. Now, these are copies that you have produced, so perhaps you could explain what's happened to the missing footnote.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what could have happened. It never crossed my mind to check the texts and to collate them and to see whether they were properly printed or not. I assumed that people did their work in the right way. And during the break, any one of my associates can mark the footnotes throughout the text so you can have all of them, although, in all fairness, there are 69 of them, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you say you assume people did their work in the proper way, which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean those who were given Professor Popov's report. How can I now collate what you have to what I have given? The paper of Professor Popov has, as an annex, footnotes, and it never crossed my mind to check whether the annex with the footnotes were -- was provided. It would be as if I checked whether all the pages were there or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you filed a submission in relation to this in response from -- to the Prosecution's motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could help us with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've only ever had it in English, and we don't have the footnotes either. So I've got a text which Your Honours have, which was provided on the 16th of August, 2004, which has got no footnotes. This, of course, has not been something that we have been dealing with on a hands-on basis at all. All we've done is shore up for the accused an opportunity to get it into evidence by making a filing on the issue of the report itself, as the Court knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are referring to people who you expect would do their work properly, and now you define these people as the people who had the report. Now, who are these people that you say somehow or other have done you a disservice by altering the form of the report which you had?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When comparing the two, the Serbian and the English, it never crossed my mind to look at the footnotes, but I don't think anything was altered. This is the first time I hear that something had been altered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question, with great respect to you. The question is: Who are the people that you suspect have done something along the way to alter this report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that anyone intentionally altered the report, and it's not any kind of change, really. Obviously, technically, the footnotes were simply not there any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unintentionally will do for me. Who are the people that you say have altered the report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make any assumptions, Mr. Bonomy, because once the report leaves my hands, I am no longer -- I mean, it's no longer in my hands. I don't control it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The person who handed it over was Mr. Ognjanovic, as far as I can see from the filing. Are you saying that through his possession of the document it has somehow or other been changed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ognjanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't think so. I did not mention Ognjanovic at all, and I cannot tell you exactly which one of my associates forwarded the document, because they take turns here. I assume that this associate of mine who forwarded the document did it in good faith as well, making every effort to do things correctly. So I can really not find fault with anyone now, but I do see now that there are no footnotes, and I find that inexplicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can find fault with yourself. You can surely do that, because the fault rests with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Serbian version's got no footnotes as well, although I've just been handed, by Ms. Anoya, a document that -- sorry -- a document that she has on file with -- oh, right. That's the professor's. Sorry, it's come round to me this way and I thought it was from her. Can I suggest that Professor Rakic, who is here at the moment and is the current associate of the accused, gets to work to put in these footnotes in the relevant passages and resubmits the report identifying those, where those passages should be, to at least correct something that I'm sure the professor would like to have completed on his behalf, the correct and appropriate footnoting of the original Serbian text and the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. But of course, Mr. Nice is disadvantaged to a certain degree in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are very substantially disadvantaged because not only has the original text been altered to excise the footnotes, and unless they were converted to end notes and wiped out in one go, that would have been many actions that were taken, but when prompted to provide a version with footnotes, neither the accused nor any of those associates of his who should have been reading filings and responding to them on his behalf took the trouble to register that we had a non-footnoted version. Now, if the footnotes don't go back in, although they won't come with all the associated documentation, that may lend some greater value to the report than it has at the moment. I'm reluctant in the extreme to ask that this witness goes away and comes back at a time when I've looked at or had a whole lot of footnotes looked at. I'm reluctant in the extreme to think of taking him into cross-examination tomorrow. I'd rather finish with him today. But if so, I'm going to finish him on the basis of the unfootnoted report with such value, if any, as it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It could be said that the concepts of this witness remain the same, and they're concepts that are well known to the Prosecution. This is not a unique case for the Prosecutor to have to deal with in this building. They're dealing with 60 of them. These are issues that are well known to the Prosecution. The fact that specific references may not be in the report is regrettable and wrong, but in my submission, it does not overly disadvantage the Prosecution in relation to dealing with the issues before it because this is a subject that it knows very, very well and perhaps the best that can be done is to try and restore the position to the most appropriate form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ultimately it will be for the Chamber to determine what weight to attach to the report and in the light of all the circumstances, one of which is the lack of footnotes. We're past the time for the break. We will rise now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me speak first. This whole episode illustrates the importance of paying attention to procedures. Had you attended to the submission from the Prosecutor, you would have picked up that there were no footnotes. You have assumed responsibility for managing your case, and any fault in this matter must be with you, must reside with you. And if I were Professor Popov, I would not accept the apology which you will no doubt offer him later on. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I saw Mr. Nice's objection, and I thought it was senseless, because it had to do with the paper of a well-known scholar and historian, and I didn't want to go into things like footnotes. And during the break, we marked all 69 footnotes in the English text. Mr. Nice will have them in front of him. He will be able to ask the professor about his sources, about everything else, because in the English text there are now all 69 footnotes. So that's been taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a matter which will go to the weight that the Chamber gives to the report, because the cross-examination will, as I said before, to a certain extent be affected. Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And we have yet to see the footnotes ourselves, and I will require some time, I hope not long, to review them when I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Professor, in light of the accused's recent observation, and indeed in light of something you said yesterday, do you take the view, as he suggests, that it would be senseless to object to the lack of footnoting, to the lack of authority of a well-known scholar and historian or do you accept that a well-known scholar and historian is susceptible to judgement based on sources, just like anyone else?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as for the methodology of scientific work in history, that is something I did during my first year at university, as a student, and I knew that even before I became a scholar myself let alone academician. So please, do not bring into question my scholarly reputation by ascribing some kind of a technical mistake to me. And I don't know myself where and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. My question to you, Professor, in light of something you said yesterday or -- yes, not yesterday, last week, when saying how your word should be accepted, my question to you is: Do you accept that your report and your evidence is as vulnerable to, as susceptible to investigation and checking as anybody else's evidence, or do you think you stand in some different league because you're an academic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Everybody's scientific paper or scholarly paper is subject to criticism, and this is not something that I wrote for eternity. It is rather -- I have it here, the manuscript, but I am going to publish it, as a matter of fact, perhaps in an expanded form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And my last question on the form of the paper, for the time being, is this: When you handed it over to the accused or to his associates, did it have footnotes or end notes?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I have it now is the way I handed it in. And I will tell you when: On the 12th of July. This complete material, footnotes included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, therefore, to excise the footnotes from the report, electronically or otherwise, would have required going through and excising individually each and every footnote. It couldn't be done by an accidental press of one button, could it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what was done. It was probably the copy with the footnotes that was mislaid somewhere. I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Can we look, please, together -- it's simply for want of time. I'm not going to pursue it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask the professor if there was a copy without footnotes or end notes somewhere that he produced to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the witness? I did not give it to him personally but to his associates in Belgrade. Possibly the copy with the footnotes was lost somewhere over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Professor, did you hand over a copy that did not have footnotes as well as a copy that did have footnotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hand in that kind of a copy, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look, please, together, at the last paragraph of your report, and I'd like you to, before we do, answer this question: Is there a duty falling on experts and academics who come to court as experts to be moderate in their use of language, Professor Popov, do you think?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language I use is always moderate. In all fairness, I've never been before a court of law, but I think that I always use moderate language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to help us with this last paragraph, and we can lay it on the overhead projector if there's an English version to spare. "What is the most tragic for the Serbian people of our times is the fact that the centuries' long myth and stereotype of Greater Serbia and that the Serb's inclination towards aggression and hegemony has been nourished, fostered and spread with incomparable force for almost a decade and a half now." Is that still your view, is it, that this myth has been nourished, fostered and spread with incomparable force? Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of insight into some books that were published in the 1990s, I come to the conclusion that this myth is still fostered. These are textbooks that were published in France first and foremost. I mention the authors here, Pierre Musin [phoen] and Serge Bernstein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we didn't have the footnotes so we'll have to look for those in a second. I'm going to read on.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't put that into the footnote, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So we would have to work that out for ourselves, would we? "Nowadays it again has its ideological basis, though in a more widespread and developed form in the theory of inequality and conflict of civilisations, the inevitability that a weaker civilisation, the eastern Byzantine to which the Serbs belong, will succumb to a stronger western Roman civilisation represented by a united Europe, United States of America, and their incomparable economic and political power." That, I imagine, is a view you still hold too?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you read Samuel Huntington's book about the Clash of Civilisations, I'm sure you will know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mention that in the next --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please take a look at the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You do mention that in the next sentence, and so you do provide a source of this, which we recognise that it's Huntington, not Haington: "From Jacob Philip Fallmereyer, who offered this solution to German imperialism, to Samuel Huntington, who offered it to the aggressive American and European globalism, all the explanations of this kind have always been the same; to conceal the aspirations of conquest of the most powerful forces in the world." So is it your opinion that this suffering of the Serbs under the myth of Greater Serbia is all the responsibility of the aspirations of those most powerful forces in the world and their desires to conquest this and this?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large extent that would be the conclusion, because the Serb people, for an entire millennium, for 1.000 years, has been subjected to similar pressures, so what is going on now is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Serbia, in your perception, has been really a victim nation and a victim state for hundreds of years, basically, hasn't it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read on: "There are numerous tendentious explanations, false accusations and rewritings of history which are currently used to attack the alleged Greater Serbdom, its aggressiveness and the genocide it carries out." So you think that those who write about -- is this right; those who write about Greater Serbdom are making false accusations, that is, deliberately false accusations? Is that your position, Professor Popov?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course one thing that an academic would always be cautious about doing would be imputing bad motives to a fellow academic because he would recognise that a fellow academic may hold different views but with -- nevertheless with good intentions, in good faith. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: And do you mean that this was presented in bad faith?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm asking you, in general, academics amongst themselves recognise they may hold differing opinions in good faith.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it would be the most extreme criticism that one academic could make of another to suggest that he or her might be holding an opinion in bad faith?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've -- I understood your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- let's read on. "All these pseudo-scientific dregs --" I don't know what the Serbian word for "dregs" is -- "of Pierre," and we don't know the name, "Serge Bernstein, Paul Garde, Allain Finkielkraut, David Risman, James Gow, Ellie Weisel, Noel Malcolm, Audrey Budding..." Let's just see if we understand what you're suggesting here, because we've seen Ms. Budding. Did you see her? Mr. Popov, did you see her?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I followed her --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... -- serious academic that it is appropriate in a report of this kind that you're going to publish as a book to describe her as a "scientific dreg"? Do you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that her report is pseudo-scientific, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to give you an opportunity to prove that, if you're up to it, but let's read on. "You name it --" please read it. Follow the text. "You name it, as well as of their Serbian lackeys have one task only, and that is to denounce 'Greater Serbian hegemony' in order to clear the path to the new world order and globalism in this part of Europe." So let's just have it. You wish this Court to assess Ms. Budding, who came from another country, not at her request, believe me, to assist this Court, and you're saying she's a dreg and a lackey; yes?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of her but of the Serb satellites going along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now justify your opinions about Ms. Budding, please, and we'll wait here until you do it. You haven't had the grace in your report to descend to particulars and to explain why you should name a fellow academic in this way, Professor Popov, so I'm going to give you a chance to do it now.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that on the basis of having read her report, from which I concluded that she does not know Serbian history very well and that the Prosecution selected the wrong man -- chose the wrong man or the wrong person for its expert. She did read Serbian history books, yes, but Serb history of the 20th century and that's what her Ph.D. is based on. However, she was very free, if I can say that, in meandering through middle -- the history of the Middle Ages and the 19th century where she isn't that well-versed, and her cross-examination of Mr. Milosevic brought that to light.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not -- that's not good enough. You're an academic calling another academic a dreg and a lackey. I want you to explain in detail how you dare make that sort of observation in what you claim to be a serious report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't think the term "lackey" is a reference to Ms. Budding, as the professor has already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's linked to him, but you're quite right. The word "dregs" will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give me some particulars, please, Professor Popov, of how you choose to describe this court expert in this way.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Ms. Budding is a member of the academy, perhaps she is, but her writings are a confusion, in fact, because she is mixing up certain medieval criteria and historical criteria from the 19th century and 21st century criteria. And it is a basic rule, or one of the basic rules of historical methodology as formulated by Dukaj, the philosopher of history, whereby every historical appearance must be looked at from the context of its own times and not from our times, because we make different judgements based on our times when we know some of the consequences of those phenomena, but they must be explained on the basis of the contemporary times. So the historian must try to relive those times, and I feel that that is lacking with Ms. Budding, and I think that that is the basic shortcoming of her work submitted to this Tribunal, because she makes a judgement of Garasanin's Nacertanije or design or plan, or Sardusin's [phoen] writings form the aspects of the 20th century and the process of globalisation, which is an ongoing one at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll look at Garasanin's Nacertanije in a minute, but you will recognise that, for the convenience of the Court, Ms. Budding's report didn't focus on the earlier history and it focused on the 20th century. I've given you a chance to be specific and you haven't taken it. We'll look at another document. May he have the declaration -- it's only in English. This is a document, I'm afraid, in English only. We'll lay it on the overhead projector. We haven't located the no doubt existing B/C/S original, but nevertheless. It would, of course, would it not -- while we're waiting for this to be displayed. It would, of course, would it not, Professor Popov, be an act of irresponsibility in the troubled times of the former Yugoslavia to put your name to a document without being able to support -- a document that might excite reaction, without being able to support what's contained in the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here's a document you put your name to, in Holy Cross Day, or on Holy Cross Day in 1997 in Belgrade, because you're signature number 36, and this is what the declaration you signed said. I don't go through all of it. If you've got it on display, that will probably be enough. If we could have it. Top of the page. "Recalls the declaration demanding that The Hague criminal charges against Radovan Karadzic be repealed," I think, "that more than a year has passed since that earliest publication;that The Hague Tribunal, since its unlawful establishment until the present day acted in a biased fashion..." Just pausing there. Do you count international law amongst your skills, Professor Popov?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know that much, that is to say that institutions of this kind of the United Nations are appointed by the General Assembly and that brings into question to a certain extent the legality of this Tribunal. So that's what I meant when I signed this text. And the second thing I thought, and that is something that I believe today, too, and it is this: That Radovan Karadzic is not a criminal --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we're going to see what you think. "Recent manoeuvres of The Hague Tribunal cannot conceal abominable crimes..." What manoeuvres? Sorry, "... abominable crimes committed by the Muslims and the Croats against the Serbs." What are the manoeuvres? You want to make allegations about this Tribunal, spell them out.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the crimes in Muslim prisons and camps, about crimes committed in the Podrinje part of Bosnia, about the torching of the Kravica village, of the major crimes in a place on the Drina called -- what was its name now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What are you suggesting? Because -- be clear. As you know, this Tribunal -- this Prosecution and this -- this Prosecutor - she's here - and this Tribunal try offences allegedly committed by all sides to this conflict. They investigate them and they try them. Now, if you have material to suggest that there's been some category of suppression, you tell us what it is. You signed this document. You weren't obliged to. You chose to.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody forced me to, of course, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "That the main aim of The Hague Tribunal is obviously to discredit, demonise, and humiliate the Serbs while pronouncing Dr. Radovan Karadzic before the trial the main culprit for war that was conducted with involvement of three parties." Is that your belief?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only do I believe it, I know it to be true. I know that the war began in Bosnia with the killing of Serbs at a funeral, at a cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pass over the next paragraph unless anybody wants me to read it out, to save time. You say: "It's already clear --" at the bottom of the page -- "that pressure exerted by international community on Dr. Radovan Karadzic is legally unfounded, has no fact nothing in common with international law." Over the page. "Pressure on Dr. Radovan Karadzic is in fact the pressure on the entire Serb people. The people's power -- the world's power mongers are trying to paralyse any political and social activity of Serbian people by completing -- by attempting to completely isolate Dr. Karadzic and continuously threatening with his arrest." And you tell us you are a serious academic. You read this document and understood its content before you put your name to it, did you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we just understand the dating? 1997. The truth of Srebrenica was before the world by 1997, Professor Popov, and the nature of the allegations made by the Tribunal set up by the United Nations were known by 1997. Do you know that there was no liability for such events as Srebrenica falling on people such as Karadzic and Mladic? Is that your position? Mladic isn't dealt with here but just Karadzic, but were you all-knowing on this matter?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: That already in 1992 and 1993, Bratunac had suffered enormously - that's the name I couldn't remember a moment ago - and that nobody lifted a finger. Now, as far as Srebrenica is concerned, that's when the news started to be disseminated, which had not been proved yet. Figures were manipulated. It started with 2.500 victims and they arrived at 9.000 victims. Yes, that's how it started out, that 2.500 civilians were killed, then 5.000, the figure was 7.000, now the figure is almost at 9.000. Which doesn't matter; the quality of crime remains the same. A crime is a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Professor Popov, your language is very important when you're an expert and an academic. The word you used was "manipulated." Your evidence, please, so that we can understand it, that the figures were manipulated as opposed to simply being the figures that emerge as more mass graves emerge. Why do you say "manipulated"?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to substantiate the call for condemnation of the accused here standing accused for genocide, and to substantiate the call for war reparations that Bosnia is asking from Serbia, and for the Serb people to be portrayed as a major criminal nation. That, in my opinion, is true manipulation, because be realistic, had 9.000 people really been killed, who would have buried all those bodies in the space of just a few days?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See if I've got it correctly. You are holding yourself out as capable of expressing an opinion to this Court on the factual accuracy of the number of people and thus the number of families bereaved in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the families who disappeared. They could have disappeared by the fact of having left and gone abroad or taken refuge in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I'm talking about the physical destruction of people, the physical victims, and I have every right to have my doubts on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to the bottom of the page to save some time, give you something where you've probably got more evidence. "The campaign against Dr. Radovan Karadzic and pressures which continuously increase have no footing in true facts. Falsifications are used as documents to impress the public, to distort the truth and to replace it with fabricated lies. Both the local and international public have been informed post festum that neither the Serbs nor Dr. Radovan Karadzic were responsible for the Markale marketplace incident. The engineers of these lies - Izetbegovic and his companions - have been exposed." Well, there's a strong statement. We know it's a controversial issue. You're an academic. What is the evidence you rely on for that very strong view on a topic that this Chamber may have to consider?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I intervene here? He's actually an academic historian giving evidence before this Court based on a report dealing with Greater Serbia. He is now being asked his opinion on other matters, presumably as an attempt by the Prosecution in some way to discredit him, but we really are getting off the area that is the subject matter of his testimony, which is the report that he submitted before the Court if we're going to ask his opinion about the Markale market massacre, if we're going to ask him his opinion about Srebrenica and all these other issues. In our submission, it may not help the Tribunal to deal with those aspects of his opinion which are within his report which are a matter of history rather than modern day politics in the form that it's being presented now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but he did sign this document, and I think the Prosecutor is entitled to test his credibility by asking him questions. Though, Mr. Nice, I hope for not much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I've really come to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to the last page and see if there's something on this page that I want your assistance with.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer your previous question about the Markale marketplace massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: In America, I think it was in Boston or maybe Chicago, there's a journal -- journal put out called Serbian Studies, which published a secret report of a military commission of SFOR which investigated, that is to say an international military commission with officers belonging to different countries, who investigated the alleged bombing of the Markale marketplace and that is a report numbering some 50 pages. I will just tell you the conclusions of that report. In conclusion, the commission states as follows, and it was handed over to the Security Council, it was never made public. The journal in some ways that I don't know how, that's why I couldn't quote, published the report, in which the conclusions made are as follows: That on that particular day on the Serb side not a single rocket was fired. On that day -- or rocket or shell, whatever -- a shell was fired from the Muslim positions. One of the members of the commission, he was a Frenchman, a French officer, even set aside his opinion claiming that there was no bomb in the first place but that the explosion came from the ground, because that's his conclusion on the basis of his on-site examination of the marketplace and the roofs of the market stalls. Now, I didn't dare, to tell you the truth, hand in that report to you because I don't have the agreement of the author of that article or the editorial board of the journal either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you remember, Professor Popov, I took you to this paragraph saying it was something where you probably have more evidence because we all know that there are competing theories about the Markale incident. What I'm interested in is to know how you, an academic, used, it appears, to weighing evidence, can act on simply one report and put your name to it in this inflammatory document. And I'm going to have a look at your footnotes in a minute if I get a couple of minutes. How could you put your name to a report like this, acting simply on a one-sided report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to wait for Mr. Nice to put his headsets back on again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not just one incident, but even that one incident that I brought up is such a serious one and heavy one that it brings all the other situations into question where Serbs have been accused. Of course, in a civil war, crimes are multiple on all sides, and to diminish the quality of a crime, whether it was 2.500 people killed, 7.000, or whatever, it means nothing. Even if there were two innocent victims killed, that is a crime, constitutes a crime. But all this has to be proved and we must not accuse in advance and ban political activity and then delve in persecutions and prosecutions until something has been proved officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite. Quite. You see I've had now your footnotes reviewed in the limited time available.
