Have you been setting out and reviewing in your report arguments and academic literature from all sides or have you been generally looking at the material that favours the conclusion that you reached, just as you did in this declaration for Karadzic, rely on the material that favoured the conclusion you wanted to reach?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took great care in following Croatian history until the last ten years. I studied French and German historiography and partially English historiography. Of course, Serbian too, that goes out saying. So all my conclusions are based on thousands of books and articles and studies read so that I cannot criticise myself on any count. And I'll tell you why I believed one source over another, for example, even though I've read different accounts. But if you would like to hear one example, I shall be happy to quote it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just finish with this declaration and then I'll turn to your footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the remaining page, frankly, is repetitious of earlier material. Can that be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the declaration demanding The Hague Tribunal criminal charges brought against Dr. Radovan Karadzic be repealed dated 1997 will be Prosecution Exhibit P803.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have dealt with the Epoha extracts first. If they could have the earlier number and this one the subsequent number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Epoha collection will be Prosecution Exhibit P803 and the declaration just referred to will be Prosecution Exhibit P804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Professor -- Professor, confining myself to the two topics, Nacertanije and the 1986 or whenever it was memorandum, can you just help me, please, by looking at your footnotes. Can you point to the literature that you've relied on and referred to in your footnotes that expresses a view on Nacertanije different from that that you have advanced so that we can know that you've dealt with it and see how you've dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Nice, this is the way it's done in historiography. You rely on a source document, an original document, no interpretation. First you read the original document and then you draw conclusions on different interpretations that were made on the basis of that. This document was published six times until now. I could have taken any one of them. I actually compared two editions, one from 1939 and the other one from 1993, and I saw that with the exception of small interventions in terms of spelling, there were no changes. However, Nacertanije was made public as far back as 1906. So there's no reason for me to look into all these other things because I read the Nacertanije itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when we come to the memorandum -- I may have to come back to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It looks as though, Your Honours, that I won't be able to finish this today but I'm very anxious to dispose of this witness in a short period of time tomorrow, which I will be able to do, I think, with, I hope, reviewing overnight the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When we come to the memorandum, I see that you refer to Kosta Mihailovic, our next witness, Vasilije Krestic, as the authors of the memorandum, but you have referred to none of the literature that is critical of the memorandum, its purpose and effect, have you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm telling you that I read the memorandum itself. I did, though, read some critiques that were published at the time, and I will give you just a brief explanation of this because I'm in a hurry, too, to tell you the truth. One of the harshest critics, as I mentioned in my paper, of the memorandum was an ex-communist high official, inter alia, Prime Minister of Serbia and foreign minister, namely Milos Minic. He accused the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, saying that they were wrong, that they will cause conflicts on the international scale, et cetera. So after all this criticism, what did he conclude? I'll quote this. Since he levelled a great deal of criticism against the memorandum, Minic could not reach any other conclusions about it except that it was an accurate diagnosis of the state of affairs in Yugoslavia in the 1980s and an astute forecast of the tragic consequences that would ensue if things continued along these lines. For me, this was a rather acceptable solution, a solution that was that was quite acceptable, as a matter of fact. When I read the memorandum, I came to the conclusion that this was a diagnosis of the state of affairs as it was and a way of getting out of that. As for an analysis of the memorandum itself, I'm sure that you're going to hear more about that tomorrow from one of its authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before I move on, one of the points in my mind: Ms. Budding, who you comment on, expressed a summary of the significance of the memorandum in this way: "It was most important as an indicator. As evidenced by 1986, the assertions it set out were accepted by influential figures within Serbia's intellectual elite." She carried on: "To put it as clearly as possible, it was the existence of the belief system set out in the memorandum rather than the memorandum itself that influenced the process of Yugoslavia's dissolution." I don't imagine you'd disagree with that conclusion of Ms. Budding, would you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've given me a brilliant example of non-historical conclusion. So you're talking about the spirit rather than the text itself. That is not what we do in historiography.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you disagree with her conclusion? Because you've been asked rather wider questions than the purely --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I disagree. It is the text that had to be proceeded from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. That's a rather sort of -- as I understand it, that's a rather normative approach to life, isn't it? You just look at the black and white letter and you don't trouble yourselves too much, or you try not to trouble yourselves too much with the effect that the black and white letters have; is that it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proceed from the methods of Leopold Ranke, who established historiography as a science. That was my first point. The second point is I do not see the memorandum as black and white letters on paper. It is actually an attempt made to replace the black by the white, if I can put it that way, if we are going to speak in metaphors now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My only dallying in the 19th century is going to be with Nacertanije because you focused on it so much.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you that you've been very partial in your analysis. It features in your proposed exhibits at tab 2 without the benefit of advantage, unless it's changed since we last spoke, of a translation. Despite that we've been able to obtain a translation off the Internet, and I'm afraid that's the best that we're going to be able to do.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've submitted Nacertanije here as an exhibit. Again there seems to have been some kind of impediment on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not your fault that it hasn't been translated, Professor Popov, don't fear. Would you accept the following three propositions: That Nacertanije promoted the idea of restoration of the Serbian borders along the lines of the medieval criterion as well as establishing the state in its ethnic borders? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one, that Serbia was promoted in its medieval borders, that is precisely proof of not looking at the Nacertanije from the point of view of that period of time. When it was written by Ilija Garasanin and Polish immigrants together, no one in the world knew what the Serbian state was and what the Serbian medieval principality was. Historiography discovered this only in the '70s and '80s. So this lived on in the consciousness of the Serbian people more as a tradition told through oral lore of epic poetry, which was highly appreciated. People thought that this empire lasted for 200 years, whereas it was only 25 years. And it did not encompass all the territories that the Nacertanije refers to. Ilija Garasanin and Chartoriski, who gave these instructions, Adam Chartoriski, they did not know that. And they invoked --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at two or three extracts from Nacertanije, so you may want to reserve your comments of detail until then. I've asked you about establishing a state in ethnic borders, and the third point I want you to deal with is whether Nacertanije also dealt with the geostrategic goal of having an outlet to the sea. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Nacertanije dealt with ethnic boundaries, and it can be proven that to the greatest degree, 90 per cent or so, Ilija Garasanin guessed well where the Serbian ethnic boundaries were on the basis of censuses in Turkey from '64, that is the so-called Xhevdet Pasha census [phoen]. It was published by Odile - I cannot refer the full name now - she's a French historian, in a Pakistani journal in 1997. Also, the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina conducted by the Austro-Hungarian authorities in 1879. If you look at all of that, you'll see that Ilija Garasanin was right when he included the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as ethnic Serbian territory, especially because Muslims at that time did not have an ethnic identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only reason I take time to deal with these points is in light of the way you've sought to diminish the notion of Greater Serbia, what we see in Garasanin's Nacertanije is reflected in the later plans, in the mid and late 20th century for Serbia, isn't it? Ethnic boundaries, medieval state --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, and you heard the examination by Mr. Milosevic. I do not recall having said at any point that Serbia in the '90s tried to implement the ideas of Ilija Garasanin, because in the meantime, during those 150 years, the situation changed considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to have to seek the usher's assistance and yours, Professor Popov, just to deal with this. We have been waiting for a translation of the Defence exhibit. It hasn't come. We've got a full translation from the Internet. It's not yet copied, but it can go on the overhead projector and we can all follow it. And if you would be good enough, please, to look at -- and I'm sorry you've got this inconvenience of not having the translated version. If you'd be good enough to go to the tab 3 of --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text that the young lady from the Registry took from me. Apparently the copy you have was a poor copy, barely legible, so she took my copy and she didn't give it back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll give you a copy because I'm going to read you the first sentence of a translation and then I'm going to ask you to find it for us in the original exhibit. Now, here comes a copy of the original exhibit, and it's probably not very far into it, and the first sentence is: "The Serbian state which has already seen its good start, but must strive to expand ..." I wonder if you can find that. Meanwhile, we'll look at it together, see if we can find it.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never mind. I can't find it. It seems that the translation does not really correspond to the original, but, yes, Garasanin did speak about the unification of Serb territories, ethnic Serb territories with the principality of Serbia. That is the essence of the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me read slowly to you, then, what's in this version of the translation and see if you agree that this reflects what Garasanin said. "The Serbian state which has already seen its good start, but must strive to expand and become stronger, has its roots and firm foundation in the Serbian Empire of the 13th and 14th centuries and in the glorious and rich Serbian history. It is known from this history that the Serbian rulers began to assume the position held by the Greek (Byzantine) Empire and almost succeeded in making an end of it in order to replace the collapsed eastern Roman Empire with a Serbian-Slavic Empire." And I'm grateful to Mrs. Tromp. The page is 153 on the original exhibit, and it's the right-hand column, and it's the first fresh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 2, indeed, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've fond it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So do you accept, as I suggested to you a little earlier, that it promotes the idea of Serbian borders along medieval lines? That simple point.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I accept that it is along medieval lines to the extent to which Chartoriski and Garasanin knew about it then. But they did not know that in the 13th and 14th century there was a Serbian Empire. There was a principality and then a kingdom and then a despot state, and so on, and the borders kept changing all the time. That the Serbian people had a glorious history, there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if the usher would be so good, and we can probably more readily now follow it in the original text, starting at page 153 of tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have this next, Professor Popov: "If we consider the revival of the Serbian Empire from this standpoint, then other South Slavs will easily understand this idea and accept it with joy; for probably no European country in the memory of the historical past so vivid as among the Slavs of Turkey, for whom the recollection is intense and faithful of the celebrated figures and events of history." It's all the same thing, isn't it? Right.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to reply to? What question should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Medieval history and medieval borders being advanced, and all lying behind the Greater Serbian concept that was to develop and be named, I think, rather later.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense in which the concept of Greater Serbia is referred to here, that is not the meaning. Bringing together the entire Serb people or its majority into one state, that is not an idea of a greater state. That is an idea that prevailed throughout Europe in the 19th century. The Serbs also had the right to espouse such an idea. The fact that he invokes medieval history is because he doesn't want to call for revolutionary methods, because he himself says we don't want to apply revolutionary methods but historical law and rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if you're looking for a time to break, but I should make this point: Time and again we are inconvenienced by not having interpreted or translated documents. With this witness I'm going to make the decision simply to reduce dramatically the questions I would otherwise have asked had I had more material because this exercise - and it's not his fault - but this exercise inevitably simply takes more time than would be taken if documentation had been properly prepared. Can I also, by way of not correction but reminder, alert the Chamber and indeed the accused to the reality that in neither of my opening speeches to this Court did I on behalf of the Prosecution rely on the words "Greater Serbia." I used the phrase once, associating it with the man Seselj, and I think on two occasions I referred to the concept of all Serbs in one state, and the phrase "Greater Serbia" which has, I think, never been attributed to the mouth of the accused is a concept that's been referred to by many other witnesses, and of course we can't control them in their analysis and understanding of events. So far as the Prosecution is concerned, it's always been careful to limit its approach to this issue to the way I opened the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in one of the indictments as well, but those, of course, preceded my openings, and my opening, in the sense for the matters of general theory and principle, supplants them, but you're quite right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you're not saying it's not an important part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. Not at all. No, it's an important -- it's an important matter to have in mind, but we've always expressed ourselves in terms of "all Serbs in one state," and we've always expressed the notion in one way or another of instrumentalising the opinions of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
